title: Squoosh Desktop: Rust image compressor for Windows & Linux
description: Compress images to AVIF, WebP, JPEG and PNG offline. The free, open-source Squoosh app for Windows and Linux, written in Rust, with batch conversion.
intro: The Squoosh image compressor as a free native app for Windows and Linux, written in Rust. Convert to AVIF, WebP, JPEG or PNG, compare side by side and batch-process whole folders, without uploading anything.
hero_alt: Squoosh Desktop comparing an original photo with an AVIF version 81% smaller
features_title: Everything Squoosh does. No browser needed.
f1_text: Your images never leave your computer. No upload, no account, no telemetry.
f2_text: MozJPEG, OxiPNG, WebP and AVIF, with every advanced setting from squoosh.app.
f3_text: Drag the divider to compare the original with the result and see how much you save.
f4_text: Convert whole folders in one go. Existing files are never overwritten.
batch_intro: squoosh.app handles one image at a time. Squoosh Desktop takes whole folders, applies your settings to every image and converts them all in one go.
b1_text: Drop a folder on the window or pick one: every image inside joins the list. Duplicate paths are ignored.
b2_text: Tick “Include subfolders” to search folders recursively, however deep the tree goes.
b3_text: Choose the codec, quality and resizing once. They apply to every image in the batch.
b4_text: Switch to “This image” to change a setting for one file only. The other fields keep following the common settings.
b5_text: Convert the whole batch with libwebp, libavif, MozJPEG or OxiPNG. Existing files are never overwritten.
b6_text: The batch runs on your computer, even offline. An error on one file does not stop the others.

a1: Squoosh.app is designed primarily for processing individual images. Squoosh Desktop adds batch processing: you can import multiple images or entire folders, apply common compression settings and convert the whole batch to AVIF, WebP, JPEG or PNG.
q2: Can I batch convert images to WebP with Squoosh?
a2: Yes. Squoosh Desktop can convert multiple images or entire folders to WebP in one batch using libwebp. The same batch workflow is available for AVIF, JPEG and PNG.
q3: Can I batch convert images to AVIF?
a3: Yes. Squoosh Desktop supports batch conversion to AVIF using libavif and AOM. You can apply the same AVIF settings to the entire batch and override settings for individual images when needed.
q4: Is there a desktop version of Squoosh?
a4: Squoosh Desktop is an independent native desktop port of Squoosh written in Rust. It is available for Windows and Linux and adds features such as folder import and batch image conversion.
a5: Yes. It is free and open-source software under the GPL-3.0-or-later license, with no ads and no account.
a6: No. Compression runs entirely on your computer, and the app works without an internet connection.
q7: What is the difference between Squoosh Desktop and squoosh.app?
a7: It has the same editor and codecs, but runs as a native app: it works offline and converts whole folders in one batch.
q8: Is Squoosh Desktop made by Google?
a8: No. Squoosh Desktop is an independent open-source project based on Squoosh by Google Chrome Labs. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by Google.

rust_intro: squoosh.app runs its encoders as WebAssembly inside a browser tab. Squoosh Desktop uses the same encoders, compiled for your processor, in an app written in Rust. It is the only desktop version of Squoosh written in Rust.
r1_text: A single executable with no bundled browser. On Windows, every build is checked to make sure it needs no third-party DLL.
r2_text: squoosh.app compiles OxiPNG, a Rust library, to WebAssembly. Here it runs as native code, the way it was written.
r3_text: libavif and AOM are built for your CPU. Previews are computed on a separate thread 300 ms after your last change, so the window keeps responding.
r4_text: JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, TIFF and SVG are read by memory-safe Rust decoders. A corrupted file gets an error message, and the batch moves on to the next one.
